extracted.intended_audience: writers, storytellers, screenwriters, filmmakers, and creators interested in craft of narrative
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating emotionally engaging, well-structured stories across mediums (film, prose, animation), emphasizing character, structure, and audience engagement. Distills Andrew Stanton's TED talk 'The Clues to a Great Story' into actionable storytelling principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make Me Care
rubrics_metrics.description: The supreme command underlying all effective storytelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories must create emotional investment; the audience should care about the characters and stakes so the story matters. (Stated as the overriding imperative.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Know Your Ending First
rubrics_metrics.description: Storytelling is 'joke telling'; understand the destination before starting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat stories like jokes — you should know the punchline (ending) so you can set up and deliver payoff. Planning the ending informs structure, setup, and the meaning of earlier events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirm Meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective narratives reinforce that life matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good story ultimately affirms meaning — it should leave the audience with a sense that what happened had significance and that life (or the characters' lives) matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make an Opening Promise
rubrics_metrics.description: "This is going to lead somewhere"; signal a worthwhile journey immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opening should promise that the narrative will go somewhere interesting and worthwhile. Early beats must suggest a trajectory and give the audience reason to stay engaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2+2 (Don't Spell Out 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences want to assemble meaning themselves; show them 2+2, don't tell them it equals 4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present pieces for the audience to connect rather than explaining every inference. Trust the audience's intelligence; allow them to put together clues and experience discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wonder
rubrics_metrics.description: The true secret ingredient to great storytelling. Find wonder in concept, story, characters; present those magical moments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek and showcase moments of awe, surprise, or delight in premise, character, or situation. Wonder is a key emotional quality that elevates a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character Spine
rubrics_metrics.description: Every character has an inner motor / dominant unconscious goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define each character's driving inner goal (their 'spine'). Examples given: WALL-E — find beauty; Marlin — prevent harm; Woody — do what's best for Andy. This inner motor should inform choices and arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop Relatable Yet Flawed Characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Likable protagonists with unfulfilled need or internal contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create protagonists who are relatable but imperfect — people with wants, needs, and contradictions. Their flaws and unmet needs generate dramatic tension and drive transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama Through Uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Build anticipation by making audiences unsure how situations will resolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate uncertainty and suspense so the audience cares about outcomes. Drama comes from not knowing what will happen and being invested enough to want resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invite Active Participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences enjoy filling gaps themselves rather than being spoon-fed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design stories that require the audience to engage mentally — infer, predict, and piece together clues — which increases involvement and satisfaction.
